scenes.visual: Title card: One Axon, Many Dendrites. Show a neuron with blue dendrites and a yellow axon; no cut or injury imagery.

scenes.tts: A neuron takes in signals on its dendrites and sends its output along its axon. These branches differ in structure and molecules. That difference is neuronal polarity. Dendrites carry receptors for neurotransmitters. The axon has its own channels and vesicle machinery. The cell must send proteins to the right place and keep them there. How does it choose an axon, then keep these domains different? Start with a young rat neuron growing in a dish.

scenes.visual: Show blue, branched, tapering dendrites receiving input and a yellow, even-width axon carrying output. Zoom into distinct molecular domains: neurotransmitter receptors on dendrites, channels and vesicle machinery in the axon. Label the distinction neuronal polarity. End on a young neuron in a culture dish. Do not show cuts or length thresholds.

scenes.tts: A rat hippocampal neuron grows several short neurites, all alike. After a day or two, one grows much faster. It becomes the axon. The others grow as dendrites. The choice behaves like a race.

scenes.visual: Label the model cultured rat hippocampal neuron. Several equal grey neurites sprout; one extends rapidly and turns yellow, then the others branch and turn blue. Remove the axotomy comparison and the 10 micrometre threshold; an unnumbered growth comparison may remain.

scenes.tts: Positive feedback makes the leader grow faster the more it grows. A lipid called P I P 3 builds up at its tip. Blocking P I 3 kinase is reported to stop axon formation. Negative feedback holds the others back. How it does that is less settled.
scenes.narration: Positive feedback makes the leader grow faster the more it grows. A lipid called PIP3 builds up at its tip. Blocking PI3-kinase is reported to stop axon formation. Negative feedback holds the others back. How it does that is less settled.
scenes.caption: Positive feedback makes the leader grow faster the more it grows. A lipid called PIP3 builds up at its tip. Blocking PI3-kinase is reported to stop axon formation. Negative feedback holds the others back. How it does that is less settled.
scenes.visual: Keep the green positive-feedback loop and PIP3 dots at the leading tip. Show PI3-kinase blockade preventing axon formation in culture. Show inhibitory marks on sibling neurites with a question mark to preserve uncertainty about the mechanism.

scenes.tts: At the growing tip, actin is looser and microtubules are more stable than in its siblings. Locally loosen actin, or stabilize microtubules, and a chosen neurite can become the axon. The cytoskeleton can tip the choice.

scenes.visual: Compare the future axon growth cone with a sibling: loose orange actin and stable teal microtubules in the future axon. In separate culture examples, locally loosen actin or stabilize microtubules in a selected neurite, then show it becoming an axon. Avoid presenting either manipulation as an inevitable outcome.

scenes.tts: Those microtubules also guide cargo. In the axon, nearly all point plus end out. In vertebrate dendrites, they point both ways. A kinesin that prefers stable, plus end out tracks can steer cargo into the axon. Dynein can carry cargo outward on minus end out tracks in dendrites. Different tracks help keep different proteins in each domain.

scenes.visual: Add parallel axon and vertebrate-dendrite insets, each with the cell-body end clearly marked. Axonal tracks are nearly all plus-end-out; dendritic tracks have mixed orientations. Animate a kinesin with the stated preference carrying cargo into the axon, and dynein carrying cargo away from the cell body along a dendritic minus-end-out track. Label motor direction and track ends; do not imply all kinesins select axonal cargo or that track direction alone fully determines sorting.

scenes.tts: Near the cell body, ankyrin G builds the axon initial segment. In many neurons, action potentials start here. It also helps hold polarity. Lower ankyrin G after the segment forms, and it falls apart. The dendrite protein M A P 2 enters the axon. The near end gains dendritic features, while farther out it keeps axonal proteins. Identity needs active maintenance.

scenes.visual: Keep the purple ankyrin-G initial segment. First show an action potential starting there, with the qualifier in many neurons. Then label a cultured neuron with an already formed initial segment; lower ankyrin G and dissolve the segment. MAP2 enters the axon; show blue coloring and dendritic spines proximally while distal axonal proteins and yellow identity remain. Distinguish maintenance from initial axon choice.

scenes.tts: In tissue, environmental cues help orient this machinery. Many cortical neurons form their axon from the trailing process during migration. Cortical neurons lacking L K B one, or both S A D kinases it activates, fail to form axons. The dish reveals mechanisms. The developing brain supplies a different starting point.

scenes.visual: Replace the closing cut-and-stump rule with a developing-cortex scene. Show a migrating neuron whose trailing process becomes the axon and environmental cues orienting polarity, without inventing specific cue molecules. Show LKB1 activating SAD-A/SAD-B, then separate loss conditions: no LKB1 or loss of both SAD kinases, each with failure to form an axon. End by comparing equal neurites in a dish with a migrating neuron in tissue. No axotomy or numerical cutoff.
End card: Neuronal polarity. Show dendritic input and axonal output with distinct molecular domains, track directions, and the initial segment visible. No axon-cutting rule.
